newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia says thousands more Khmer Rouge defect.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia says thousands more Khmer Rouge defect.

text.p: More than 2,000 Khmer Rouge guerrillas told the Cambodian government on Friday they were defecting from hardline forces, senior military officials said.

"There are more Khmer Rouge defections today of up to 2,017 troops and 3,982 families numbering 18,465 people," Em Mara, a senior defence ministry official based in the northwest province of Battambang, said.
Em Mara said the rebels were based in the southwest province of Koh Kong, the western province of Pursat and around the northwest town of Samlaut.
He said the guerrillas had contacted military officers by radio on Friday morning and asked to be recognised as government troops. They later sent the request in writing.
It was not clear to which divisions the defectors belonged.
The numbers, if confirmed, would bring to almost 5,000 the number of guerrillas claimed by the military to have defected to the government since the beginning of the month.
"This is another success of the government," Co-Defence Minister Tea Banh told Reuters.
"I hope the Khmer Rouge soldiers around and in Anlong Veng will come to defect sooner or later," he said of the remaining stronghold of hardline guerrillas loyal to Pol Pot.
Pol Pot was the leader of the 1975-79 "killing fields" regime during which more than one million Cambodians died from execution, starvation or overwork.

The town of Samlaut was seized from hardliners late last month by fighters loyal to Ieng Sary, the foreign minister during Pol Pot's regime. He broke away from hardliners loyal to Pol Pot in August and opened peace talks with the government.

Ieng Sary and his commanders in northwest Cambodia have been taking a cautious approach to full reconciliation with the government, saying the process of merging their forces with the army and opening up of their areas needs more time and trust.

His commanders have criticised the government's General Keo Pong, who defected from the Khmer Rouge earlier this year and has been instrumental in brokering the defections, for bypassing the dissident faction to join the royalist government.
A western analyst said Keo Pong and Ei Chien, commander of dissident stronghold of Pailin, maintain a sharp rivalry over who can gather the most troops for their side.
Ei Chien was eager to add to the Ieng Sary breakaway faction to increase its bargaining position with the government, analysts said.
The Maoist Khmer Rouge movement has been savaged by Ieng Sary's split and the defections, which come five years after the guerrillas signed a U.N. brokered peace pact with rival factions.
The Khmer Rouge later reneged on the pact and had been fighting the coalition government formed after 1993 elections.
